claim_verdicts.evidence: Executed 2026-09-27 on postgres:17.6-alpine (version(): PostgreSQL 17.6), throwaway DB loaded from stage-0 db/schema.sql + db/seed.sql (ff911b0). SELECT count(*) over customers LEFT JOIN orders LEFT JOIN payments -> 13 (1 row). Seed: 12 orders, payments.order_id values 1,2,3,5,7,8,10,11 all distinct; customer 5 in no order.

stage-0 db/seed.sql: orders 1, 2, 10 have customer_id 1; payments (1,order 1,2150000,card), (2,order 2,890000,card), (7,order 10,1730000,card). Run: Trần Minh Anh payments_made 3, paid_vnd 4770000 = 2150000+890000+1730000.
PG17 §9.21: "Aggregate functions compute a single result from a set of input values." Table 9.60 lists count, sum, avg, min, max.

Table 9.60: count(*) "Computes the number of input rows."; count("any") "Computes the number of input rows in which the input value is not null." Run confirms: customer 5 rows_in_group 1, payments_made 0.
§9.18.2: "The COALESCE function returns the first of its arguments that is not null."

SELECT Description: step 2 FROM list computed; 3 WHERE eliminates rows; 4 rows combined into groups, aggregates computed, HAVING eliminates groups; 5 "The actual output rows are computed using the SELECT output expressions"; 8 ORDER BY sorts. The page describes this as "general processing", which the claim's 'not the server's plan' qualifier matches.
§7.2.2/§2.7: WHERE cannot contain aggregates (fetched summary). Run: WHERE sum(p.amount_vnd) > 2000000 -> ERROR:  aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE.

§7.2.3: GROUP BY groups "rows in a table that have the same values in all the columns listed"; "The effect is to combine each set of rows having common values into one group row that represents all rows in the group." SELECT step 4: aggregates computed per group. Run: 13 rows -> (5 rows).

SELECT GROUP BY clause: not valid to refer to ungrouped columns "except within aggregate functions or when the ungrouped column is functionally dependent on the grouped columns... A functional dependency exists if the grouped columns (or a subset thereof) are the primary key of the table containing the ungrouped column." Run: SELECT c.id, c.full_name, c.email ... GROUP BY c.id succeeded, 5 rows.

SELECT HAVING clause: "HAVING eliminates group rows that do not satisfy the condition... Each column referenced in condition must unambiguously reference a grouping column, unless the reference appears within an aggregate function or the ungrouped column is functionally dependent on the grouping columns."

Executed 2026-09-27 on postgres:17.6-alpine (version(): PostgreSQL 17.6), throwaway DB loaded from stage-0 db/schema.sql + db/seed.sql (ff911b0). psql --echo-queries -f revenue-by-customer.sql: first result paid_vnd 6400000 (Phạm Thu Hà), 4870000, 4770000, 3150000, 0; footer (5 rows).

SELECT page: "An output column's name can be used to refer to the column's value in ORDER BY and GROUP BY clauses, but not in the WHERE or HAVING clauses; there you must write out the expression instead." Run: HAVING paid_vnd > 1 -> ERROR:  column "paid_vnd" does not exist.
Run: ... GROUP BY c.full_name HAVING p.method='card' -> ERROR:  column "p.method" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function. Matches SELECT page HAVING rule.

issues.text: Vũ Gia Khánh's one row has NULL in p.amount_vnd, and Nguyễn Bảo Châu's group also has a NULL-amount row yet her total is a number. That sum skips NULL is only stated in Connections; in the body I had to infer it from the count(p.id) sentence.
issues.fix: Change "His `sum` has no values to add" to "`sum`, like `count(p.id)`, skips `NULL`, so his `sum` has no values to add".
issues.quote: His `sum` has no values to add and returns `NULL`, not zero, and `coalesce` is what turns that into the `0` the shop can read.

issues.text: "those same columns" read to me as the GROUP BY columns only, so the second query's `HAVING sum(p.amount_vnd) > 2000000` briefly looked illegal until section 5 said "HAVING only grouped columns and aggregates".
issues.fix: Change "and `HAVING` may name only those same columns" to "and `HAVING` follows the same rule: grouped columns, or columns inside an aggregate".
issues.quote: `SELECT` may name only a column that is listed in `GROUP BY` or wrapped in an aggregate, and `HAVING` may name only those same columns.

issues.text: Re-read twice: the paragraph covers aggregates, HAVING as last filter, when output names exist, ORDER BY accepting them, HAVING rejecting them, then sorting. The two ORDER BY sentences are split by the HAVING one.
issues.fix: Move "`ORDER BY` sorts the rows that are left." to directly after "are computed only now, after `HAVING`.", and keep the ORDER BY/HAVING naming sentence last.
issues.quote: `ORDER BY` accepts those names; `HAVING`, like `WHERE`, does not, so there you write the expression out again. `ORDER BY` sorts the rows that are left.

issues.text: Answered a correctly, but the explanation's last sentence points me to "after the grouping step", i.e. HAVING — and section 5 says `p.method = 'card'` in HAVING is rejected. I leave the question unsure where the condition could go at all.
issues.fix: Replace the last sentence of the correct explanation with one inside the lesson, e.g. "A row filter in WHERE cannot pick customers without also shrinking their totals."
issues.quote: A condition that must not touch the totals belongs after the grouping step, not before it.
